tone_statements.citation: Ngun Tin Par. 2016. Agreement and Verb Stem Alternation in Senthang Chin. MA thesis, Payap University, Chiang Mai. xii+194 pp. (Glottolog grammar sketch; Phaipha/central dialect)
tone_statements.quote: There are three tones in the Phaipha dialect: high (i.e. /tsʰɘ́/ ‘blood’), mid (i.e. /tsʰɘ/ ‘wind’), and low (i.e. /tsʰɘ̀ / ‘slide’). The vernacular writing system does not mark tone.
tone_statements.locator: p. 321, footnote 2; grammatical tone at p. 323 (pronouns), p. 325 (Set 1 subject agreement markers, Table 5), p. 327 (Set 3 markers), p. 328 (Table 8 comparison)

sources.note: Nothing. Sec. 3.2 'Phonology' (pp. 25-27), explicitly 'very preliminary and based loosely on' Craft & Craft (2012): consonant and vowel charts, three contrasting tones (High/Mid/Low, minimal triplet 'blood/wind/slide'), tone used grammatically (plural pronouns, tense, imperative, transitivity), syllable formula 'C V (V) (C) (C) T'. No mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent full text: only discourse 'prominence').

tone.says: States first-hand that the Phaipha (central) dialect of Senthang has three contrastive tones, high / mid / low, with a minimal triplet /tsʰɘ́/ 'blood', /tsʰɘ/ 'wind', /tsʰɘ̀/ 'slide' (p. 321 n. 2), unmarked in the orthography. The body uses tone grammatically: 'The first syllable of any plural pronoun bears low tone while that of a singular pronoun bears high tone' (p. 323); for Set 1 subject agreement markers 'the only difference between the subject singular and plural.. is tone. sources.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2023. Tone in South Central Tibeto-Burman. Himalayan Linguistics 22(1): 36-66.
sources.note: Second-hand: Senthang 'described as having' only level pitches with a three-level L/M/H distinction (citing Ngun Tin Par 2016); mentions the minor syllable tsə 'anymore' taking L or H by leftward tone spread (Ngun Tin Par 2016: 58). No word-stress statement.

sources.citation: Lotven, Samson. 2021. [IU Bloomington PhD dissertation on Zophei / Maraic sound systems], sec. 2.5 'Senthang overview' (pp. 33-35).
sources.note: Second-hand summary of Ngun Tin Par 2016/Watson 2019: three register tones H/M/L (tʰə́ 'blood', tʰə̄ 'wind', tʰə̀ 'slide'), 7 vowels, coda inventory; notes 'much work needs done.. especially in terms of the sound system'. No stress statement.

sources.citation: Lotven, S., K. Berkson, J. C. Wamsley, J. Danaher, K. Van Bik & S. Davis. 2020. The syllable in Kuki-Chin. Journal of South Asian Languages and Linguistics (aop). doi:10.1515/jsall-2019-2014
sources.note: Cites Senthang (Par 2016) only for segmental/syllable facts (nasal codas /m n ŋ/, no lateral affricates, no /hŋ/); nothing on stress.

sources.note: Nothing on word stress. Sec. 1.7 'Phonology and orthography' (pp. 8-9), based on Ngun Tin Par 2016 and Craft & Craft 2012: 24 consonants, 9 vowels, 'three tones in Senthang: high, mid, and low' with grammatical tone alternations. 'Stress/accent' occur only in the discourse-literature review (Givon/Chafe on stressed vs unstressed pronouns), not about Senthang phonology.

sources.note: Second-hand only (held Watson 2019 text, sec. 1.9.6 'Verbal inflection', p. 20): 'There seem to be “at least” three sets of postverbal subject agreement markers according to Ngun Tin Par (2019). Phonologically, they are similar, although the tone differs between them.' So the 2019 sketch, as Watson reports it, distinguishes agreement-marker sets by tone (grammatical tone, tone-marked paradigms in Watson's Tables 11-13 adapted from it); whether it contains a tone-inventory/phonology section remains unverified - manuscript not seen.
